person.persName: snar thang bsam gtan bzang po
snar thang pa bsam gtan bzang po
bcom ldan rigs pa'i ral gri
person.note: On his career, see [KHA9ZVGP]: 3-8. The dates 1227-1305 are known from the biography (see work (ID:7016)) composed by his student bSam gtan bzang po (ID:4005) ([KHA9ZVGP]: 3). His name in religion was Dar ma rgyal mtshan or Chos kyi rgyal mtshan ([FZ6N88AU]: 406) - the name Chos kyi rgyal mtshan is given as his "real name" (mtshan dngos) in a homage by Rong ston ([KM47ZZDJ]: 657 and n. 62). The majority of the colophons of his works name him "bCom ldan ral gri," a few "Rigs/Rig pa’i ral gri" or just "Ral gri." Schwabland's discussion of the variants “Rigs pa” and “Rig pa” does not come to a definite conclusion as to which is the correct spelling ([CTQMVBPR]: 2-3). He was born as the son of a local wealthy headman, the fourth of five sons and his birth is reported to have been foretold by Śākyaśrībhadra (ID:6418) when he was invited by Ral gri's paternal uncle ([KHA9ZVGP]: 3).

person.persName: mkhan chen blo bzang grags pa
dka' bzhi pa shes rab seng ge
person.note: If one adopts 1333 as the date for his commentary on monastic discipline (ID:7861), and 1356 for that of bSam gtan bzang po, work (ID:4735), that refers to him in its colophon, this Shes rab seng ge must be different from rGyud smad shes rab seng ge (1383-1445) (ID:4123).

bibl.title: me tog phreng rgyud kyi TIk+ka legs bshad rgya mtsho
མེ་ཏོག་ཕྲེང་རྒྱུད་ཀྱི་ཊཱིཀྐ་ལེགས་བཤད་རྒྱ་མཚོ
bibl.author: snar thang bsam gtan bzang po
bibl.note:
Date of composition: lo sum stong bzhi brgya dgu bcu rtsa gsum pa'i dus su | gdong ngan gyi lo sa ga'i dkar phyogs tshes brgyad (the eigth day of Vaiśākha śūkla pakṣa (Buddha's birthday), male fire monkey year) = 1356, 1416/17 or 1476. [N77QW83A]: 187, n. 156 adopts the date 1356.
The work is based on the teaching of dKa' bzhi pa Shes rab seng ge (ID:3860). If the work dates from 1356, this Shes rab seng ge cannot be rGyud smad Shes rab seng ge (ID:4123) (1383-1445).
This commentary on the vinayakārikā mālākāra - one of the three that survived - is discussed in [N77QW83A]: 186-189, n. 156 and [UGZJBIWM]: 374-375.
